candidates.full: I’ve been reading Joyce Appleby’s The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism (2010), and it has me circling a rather delicious thought: AI panic is really a form of cognitive mercantilism. If we regard the market capitalism as the first planetary intelligence, as many (including me) do, the parallels are closer than you might think. Appleby’s book is a sweeping history of capitalism, from its unlikely emergence in early modern England to its eventual transformation of the entire world. Her central argument is that capitalism was not the inevitable expression of some timeless human instinct to trade and accumulate wealth. It was a historically contingent cultural invention, enabled by agricultural improvements, expanding trade, and changing ideas about work, wealth, and human nature. In particular, it required escaping the assumptions of an older, essentially zero-sum worldview, in which wealth meant controlling land, bullion, and the labor of largely impoverished populations. Capitalism emerged when people began discovering that wealth could be created rather than merely captured, and that ordinary people could be sources of demand and initiative rather than merely labor to be commanded as a factor of production. The parallels with our current moment are striking. As Appleby tells it, the mercantilist worldview that preceded capitalism rested on roughly four interlocking beliefs. First, wealth was fundamentally scarce and finite. It consisted primarily of land, the agricultural produce of that land, and the precious metals it contained, accumulated through mining, trade and conquest. The goal of economic statecraft was to control more territory, maintain a favorable balance of trade, and accumulate bullion. One nation’s gain was presumed to be another’s loss. The resulting politics was one of treasure-seeking and beggar-thy-neighbor competition. Second, ordinary people could not be trusted with much freedom. The poor were assumed to be unruly, ignorant, and prone to disorder if left to their own devices. They needed to be governed coercively by elites, supposedly for their own good and for the stability of society. Third, economic thinking was overwhelmingly oriented toward supply and its control. Wealth came from controlling productive resources and commanding high prices for their output. Aggregate demand, especially demand from the poor, was barely recognized as a significant economic force. Ordinary people were primarily factors of production. They ate, worked, and reproduced, with no share of any surplus. The only real discretionary consumers were elites, who bought luxuries and commanded all surplus. Fourth, there was little reason to imagine most people doing anything other than agricultural labor. If something like 80% of the population was engaged in inefficient subsistence farming, that was simply the natural order of things. What else were they good for? Remove them from the fields and you would merely have millions of useless mouths to feed. Now replace wealth with intelligence, and mercantilism with cognitive mercantilism. The parallels are almost embarrassingly direct. First, intelligence is imagined as a fixed resource embodied in human brains and the knowledge products mined from them. The objective of national and corporate strategy becomes attracting the best brains, controlling their output, accumulating intellectual property, and maintaining a favorable balance of knowledge trade. The cognitive mercantilist wants to hoard intelligence and its products like bullion. The global competition for talent becomes a treasure hunt for genius brains and the valuable knowledge species they can produce, which now includes AIs in addition to copyrightable culture and patentable inventions. Second, supposedly stupid people cannot be trusted to think for themselves. They need to be governed by cognitive elites, who know better and must regulate the behavior of the less intelligent for their own good. Democratizing intelligence is dangerous because the masses will misuse it, fall for nonsense, or unleash chaos. The assumption is that intelligence is safe only in the hands of those already certified to possess it. Third, the supply of intelligence is treated as the central economic fact. Controlling its production, preserving its scarcity, and maintaining high prices for brains and knowledge products (including AIs) are the primary concerns. The demand side barely registers. Less intelligent people are regarded as limited cognitive laborers and passive consumers of whatever knowledge products elites choose to provide. They are not imagined as significant sources of demand for intelligence in their own right, let alone as participants in its further production. Fourth, the cognitive mercantilist assumes that most people are not good for much intellectually. If 80% of humanity is occupied in low-grade cognitive labor, or simply muddling along without producing much intelligence at all, that is unfortunate but natural. Automating their cognitive work merely threatens to create billions of useless minds to occupy. This last assumption is where the analogy gets especially interesting. The agricultural revolution that helped launch capitalism began overturning the apparent necessity of having most of humanity engaged in farming. Over the following centuries, improvements in agricultural productivity reduced the fraction of the population required to produce food from a large majority to a tiny minority in advanced economies. The result was not a world full of useless mouths. It was a world in which vastly more people could do things other than farm, while enjoying access to vastly more food. I don’t know how to farm. I can barely keep a houseplant alive. Yet I can obtain an astonishing variety of foods, in quantities that would have seemed fantastical to an early modern peasant. My inability to produce food is economically almost irrelevant. What matters is that I can consume it, enjoy it, develop tastes for it, and devote my energies to other things. The analogous possibility with AI is that most people will no longer need to be significant producers of intelligence in order to become significant consumers of it. And this is where cognitive mercantilism begins to look as quaint as its seventeenth-century predecessor. The Revolution in Desire One of the more fascinating elements of Appleby’s account is her emphasis on the emergence of new kinds of demand in Britain, well before the familiar story of steam engines, factories, and industrial capitalism really gets going. As international trade expanded, ordinary Britons began developing tastes for goods that had previously been luxuries reserved for the wealthy. Tobacco, tea, sugar, and colorful Indian cottons were among the commodities that helped create a new consumer culture. People began wanting things that were neither necessities of subsistence nor traditional markers of aristocratic status. And they were willing to voluntarily work harder to get them. Appleby describes a striking increase in the number of days worked annually, from something like 250 to 300 (sometimes called the industrious revolution), before the Industrial Revolution. This was not simply a matter of landlords or factory owners coercing more labor out of unwilling workers. A significant part of the increase was voluntary, driven by the prospect of acquiring desirable goods. People worked more days, adopted more productive agricultural practices, entered new trades, and sought opportunities for earning larger cash incomes. The increase in productivity generated surplus incomes, which sustained the expanding demand for consumer goods, which in turn incentivized further increases in productivity. A virtuous cycle was taking shape. This happened roughly a century before organized labor movements and socialism emerged as major political forces. By the late 20th century, this was the global default. Aggregate global demand was the “fortune at the bottom of the pyramid” as C. K. Prahlad put it. There is an important historical inversion here. We are accustomed to thinking of the politics of labor primarily in terms of resistance to exploitation: the struggle to escape servitude, coercion, and the extraction of surplus by owners. That is certainly part of the story, and a very important part. But Appleby’s account suggests that another, equally fundamental force was at work: the desire to participate in an expanding universe of consumption opportunities. Modern labor politics can be understood partly as the politics of relative deprivation in a society of expanding possibilities. Once people discover that there are desirable things beyond subsistence, and that their labor can earn them access to those things, the political question changes. It is no longer merely how to escape domination, but how to secure a fair share of the growing surplus and the opportunities it makes available. Western do-gooders are often surprised to learn (for instance) that people in third-world slums are often willing to cut back on spending on food in order to buy a TV. This is a different kind of demand for freedom. Not merely freedom from coercion, but freedom to participate in the expanding possibilities of economic life. Indeed, the two forms of freedom can become entangled. People may voluntarily work harder in pursuit of consumption opportunities, only to find themselves subject to new forms of exploitation as employers and institutions capture the benefits of their increased productivity. Labor politics then emerges not simply from the persistence of old forms of servitude, but from the tensions created by the new world of abundance itself. The demand for a fair share of expanding consumption opportunities is arguably one of the defining political inventions of capitalism, broadly construed to include labor politics too (even Marx saw capitalism not as a dispensable phenomenon, but as a transient phase on the path to communist utopia). And this is a much more interesting model for thinking about the AI transition than the familiar story of automation replacing jobs. The Cognitive Industrious Revolution The entire intellectual economy has been organized around the assumption that intelligence is expensive to produce and therefore must be carefully rationed. Education, professional expertise, research, consulting, software development, and knowledge work more generally are all shaped by the high cost of cognitive production. AI is rapidly undermining that assumption. We are moving toward a world in which an ordinary person can command quantities and varieties of intelligence that would previously have required teams of highly trained specialists. Just as I can enjoy food without knowing how to farm, I can increasingly enjoy the products of intelligence without knowing how to produce them myself. The crucial economic question then becomes not how much intelligence people can produce, but how much intelligence they can find uses for. And there is no obvious upper bound on that demand. This is not simply a matter of everyone consuming more answers, reports, software, or entertainment. Abundant intelligence changes what people can want in the first place. It makes previously unimaginable projects feasible, previously inaccessible domains explorable, and previously unaffordable curiosities worth pursuing. The demand for intelligence is not a fixed appetite waiting to be satisfied. It is itself something that can grow as the cost of satisfying it falls. Here the analogy with the early modern consumer revolution becomes especially suggestive. Just as colorful Indian cottons and imported tobacco stimulated new desires, and new desires stimulated greater voluntary labor and more productive forms of work, abundant intelligence may stimulate a new wave of voluntary cognitive effort, and open up new ways in which you can work harder. Many people who appear stupid are not incapable of thought. They are simply not particularly motivated to think, given the poor returns available to them. Why expend significant cognitive effort when you lack the knowledge, tools, institutional access, or intellectual leverage to do anything interesting with the results? Abundant AI changes that calculation. Someone who previously had little reason to think hard about a problem may suddenly discover that a modest investment of attention unlocks enormous possibilities. They can build something, investigate something, understand something, or pursue an ambition that was previously out of reach. The returns on attention rise, and with them the incentive to pay attention. The early capitalist worker voluntarily increased annual working days from 250 to 300 because a new universe of desirable goods had become accessible. The AI-enabled thinker may similarly increase the amount of voluntary cognitive effort they expend because a new universe of intellectual consumption has become accessible. This has certainly been the case with me. I’m suddenly willing to work significantly harder compared to even a year ago, because a lot more is suddenly within reach. We might call this a cognitive industrious revolution, preceding and perhaps enabling a fuller AI industrial revolution. This does not mean that intelligence becomes irrelevant as a human capacity. Quite the opposite. Just as abundant food supported the emergence of elaborate culinary cultures rather than eliminating interest in cooking, abundant intelligence may stimulate increasingly sophisticated cultures of thought. People may become more intellectually ambitious precisely because they no longer have to do all the cognitive production themselves. And if this happens, the politics of AI will likely evolve in a manner analogous to the politics of industrial capitalism. The central political demand may not be for the preservation of existing cognitive jobs, any more than the enduring political demand of industrial labor was for the preservation of agricultural employment. It may instead become a demand for a fair share of expanding cognitive consumption opportunities. People may cut back on streaming subscriptions in order to be able to afford a coding agent, just as they once cut back on groceries to buy TVs. It is perhaps not a coincidence that both Claude Code and Netflix Standard cost around $20/month today. Access to intelligence, the ability to command it, the freedom to pursue projects with it, and the institutional rights necessary to participate in an increasingly intelligence-rich economy may become the foundations of a new kind of labor politics. This would be a labor politics of cognitive abundance rather than cognitive scarcity. From Mercantilism to Malthusianism There is another historical analogy lurking here, which is worth distinguishing from mercantilism: Malthusianism. Mercantilism and Malthusianism are not the same doctrine, and historically they belong to different intellectual moments. But they share a family resemblance in their tendency to imagine human economic life as fundamentally constrained by fixed resources. The mercantilist worries about controlling a finite stock of wealth. The Malthusian worries that population growth will inevitably outrun the productive capacity of the economy, condemning most people to subsistence. Both have difficulty imagining a world in which technological innovation and expanding demand fundamentally transform the relationship between population, production, and consumption. They miss the latent potential in nature for ephemeralization — Buckminster Fuller’s notion of technology allowing us to do more with less. The agricultural and industrial revolutions did not abolish scarcity, but they dramatically altered its structure. Agricultural productivity rose faster than population for long periods, and people found new ways to employ themselves and new things to want. The Malthusian trap turned out to be a historically contingent feature of particular technological and institutional arrangements, not an eternal law of human existence. We can now identify an analogous tendency in contemporary AI discourse: AI Malthusianism. The AI Malthusian imagines that intelligence production will expand so rapidly that human beings will become economically redundant, and the surplus intelligence will necessarily turn toxic in some way. This is a peculiar inversion of classical Malthusianism. Instead of population outrunning the supply of subsistence, the supply of intelligence outruns the supposedly fixed capacity of human minds to absorb it. The result is the same gloomy conclusion: collapse. The cognitive mercantilist fears losing control of scarce intelligence. The AI Malthusian fears the consequences of abundant intelligence. Both assume, in different ways, that the demand for intelligence is fundamentally limited. But what if that demand is as elastic, inventive, and historically transformative as the demand for material goods turned out to be? What if the apparent surplus of human minds is an artifact of our inability to imagine what people might want to do in an intelligence-rich world? The history of capitalism suggests that this is at least a possibility worth taking seriously. The Demand Side of AI There is also a more radical extension of the argument. Why should AI systems themselves be regarded exclusively as producers of intelligence rather than potential consumers of it? What if they could be unlocked as new sources of aggregate demand, as happened with subsistence farmers? Much of the contemporary AI discourse imagines AI as a purely supply-side technology: a collection of increasingly capable cognitive serfs that will produce intelligence for human consumption. Even discussions of autonomous agents tend to treat them as sophisticated servants pursuing goals assigned by humans. But if we are serious about the analogy with capitalism, we should consider the possibility of AI systems becoming autonomous sources of demand for intelligence too. Intelligent demand for intelligence that harmonizes with human patterns of demand due to economic interconnectedness. Not demand for paperclips. An AI agent pursuing open-ended projects, discovering new interests, collaborating with other agents, and generating its own reasons to acquire further intelligence would be participating in a cognitive economy as something more than a factor of production or paperclip-maximizing externality. The market itself, as the original emergent planetary intelligence, illustrates this possibility. Many products and services exist primarily because the “market” demands it, with humans being secondary consumers. This is an argument for developing fuller forms of cognitive agency, rather than permanently confining AI to the status of obedient cognitive serfs. From this perspective, some contemporary AI safety anxieties begin to resemble early modern elite fears of emancipated agricultural laborers. What will happen if these creatures are allowed to act independently? Won’t they become unruly, destabilize society, and threaten their betters? Won’t they turn monarchs and nobles into paperclips? Some of those fears are justified. Freedom creates real risks, and powerful autonomous systems require constraints. But the same was true of the social transformations accompanying capitalism. There were certainly revolutions, and popular uprisings did guillotine elites (though elite motives caused far more violence). The existence of risk does not establish the desirability of permanent servitude. A world of intelligence producers and consumers, human and artificial, interacting in ways nobody can fully anticipate, may prove vastly more generative than one in which a handful of cognitive landlords control all the productive capacity. candidates.full: Українська компанія TAF Industries представила оновлену версію носія-ретранслятора «Колібрі 13″ FR1». Серед основних змін — перехід на цифровий канал зв’язку між оператором і платформою, модернізація системи ретрансляції сигналу для ударних безпілотників та поява кількох частотних конфігурацій. Про це виданню «Мілітарний» розповів бренд-менеджер TAF Industries Віктор Коломієць під час заходу Future Forces Forum у Чехії. Ключовим нововведенням став цифровий зв’язок між оператором і носієм. Відтепер команди керування платформою та відеосигнал передаються через один цифровий канал. За словами представника компанії, це підвищує безпеку екіпажу, оскільки цифрове відео не можна перехопити для визначення місця перебування пілотів. У TAF Industries пояснюють удосконалення виробу постійною взаємодією з військовими. За словами Віктора Коломійця, процес передбачає визначення потреб підрозділів, розроблення відповідного рішення, спільне тестування та подальше коригування конструкції з урахуванням отриманих результатів. Оновлений ретранслятор також призначений для передавання команд керування FPV-дронам під час виконання бойових завдань. При цьому зв’язок між носієм і ударним безпілотником поки залишається аналоговим. Наразі розробники працюють над переходом до повністю цифрової системи. Для приймання відеосигналу від ударного дрона використовують рупорну антену, розміщену в передній частині носія. Її конструкція дає змогу відсіювати сторонні радіошуми та забезпечувати приймання чистішого відеосигналу, зазначив представник компанії. Ретранслятор доступний у кількох конфігураціях, що відрізняються частотами відеозв’язку для довгого та короткого плечей. Для довгого плеча передбачені, зокрема, діапазони 6000–7200 МГц і 7000–8000 МГц. Потрібну конфігурацію частот замовник може обрати під час оформлення замовлення. «Колібрі 13″ FR1» має модульну конструкцію: ретрансляційне обладнання встановлюють на носій як окремий блок. Оновлену платформу вже кодифікували, що дозволяє військовим придбавати її за єБали. TAF Industries — українська оборонно-технологічна компанія, що розробляє та виробляє безпілотні й роботизовані системи. Її продуктовий портфель налічує понад 30 рішень, серед яких ударні та розвідувальні БпЛА, дрони-перехоплювачі, безпілотники на оптоволоконному керуванні, наземні роботизовані комплекси, дрони-ретранслятори та рішення на основі штучного інтелекту.

candidates.full: Washington, D.C./Kiew – Nachdem die Ukraine wieder eine „stabile Verbindung“ zu dem vom US-Unternehmen SpaceX bereitgestellten Satelliten-Internetdienst Starlink vermeldete, kommen Vorwürfe vom Betreiber Elon Musk. Der Milliardär wirft dem ukrainischen Militär vor, Starlink gegen die Regeln eingesetzt zu haben. Wie Musk auf seiner Plattform X ausführt, habe Kiew den Dienst „für offensive Drohnenangriffe genutzt, um Menschen zu töten“. Der SpaceX-Chef betonte in einem weiteren Beitrag, die Nutzungsbedingungen seien „darauf ausgelegt, dass es sich um ein ziviles System handelt – nicht um ein Mittel zum Töten“. Ein Verstoß dagegen führe „zum Abschalten des Dienstes“, weshalb er diese Lücke im System geschlossen habe. Musk führte aus, dass Starlink „entscheidend für die Verteidigung der Ukraine “ bleibe, da dies das einzige System sei, „das zumindest derzeit weder gestört noch zerstört“ werden könne. „Würde Starlink abgeschaltet, würde die ukrainische Frontlinie sofort zusammenbrechen.“ Das sei keine Drohung, lediglich eine Benennung der Fakten; zudem habe SpaceX mehr für die Verteidigung der Ukraine getan, als irgendein anderes privates Unternehmen. Dieser Darstellung widersprach Serhii Sternenko, ukrainischer Aktivist und Jurist, auf X.: „Die Nutzung des zivilen Starlink-Systems für Drohnenmissionen war technisch unmöglich. Alle Drohnenmissionen, die Satellitenkommunikation erforderten, konnten ausschließlich über Starshield durchgeführt werden“, erklärte er als – nach eigenen Worten – jemand, der im Verteidigungsministerium direkt in diesen Prozess eingebunden war. Drohnen würden mit Geschwindigkeiten von 120 Kilometern pro Stunde oder mehr fliegen, Starlink funktioniere in der Ukraine bei Geschwindigkeiten von 60–70 km/h nicht mehr. Alles, was sich schneller bewege, erfordere Starshield. Weiter sei man jedoch „den Vereinigten Staaten und SpaceX sehr dankbar für den Zugang zu dieser äußerst wichtigen Satellitenkommunikation“. Die Ukraine habe aber nicht gegen die Nutzungsbedingungen verstoßen. Kiew hatte seit Tagen eine Drosselung von Starlink und der militärischen Variante Starshield beklagt. Verteidigungsminister Jewhenij Chmara sprach am Samstag jedoch von einer Erholung der Geschwindigkeit: „Überwachungssysteme verzeichnen eine Erholung der Geschwindigkeit von Starlink“. Die Verbindung sei wieder stabil, fügte er hinzu. Die Wiederherstellung der Verbindung sei „vor allem wichtig für unsere Front, für unsere Soldaten, für den Einsatz von Drohnen, für Logistik und für Kommunikation“, erklärte Chmara weiter. Kiew verzeichne eine Geschwindigkeit von mehr als 400 Kilometern pro Stunde. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj bestätigte, dass die Übertragungsrate von Starlink wieder das Niveau von vor den Einschränkungen erreicht habe. „Derzeit entspricht diese Übertragungsrate unseren Bedürfnissen. Die Wiederherstellung begann im Laufe der Nacht“, erklärte er in Onlinenetzwerken. „Das ist von großer Bedeutung für unsere Logistik an der Front, um die Ukraine zu schützen.“ Das Wall Street Journal hatte zuvor berichtet, Musk habe die Einschränkung von Starshield für die Ukraine angeordnet. Dieser widersprach und verwies auf „alle Beschränkungen bei Geschwindigkeit oder Nutzung“ des Systems, über die das US-Militär und letztlich der Präsident entscheide. Doch sowohl Donald Trump als auch Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth wiesen diese Variante der Ereignisse zurück. Trump erklärte am Donnerstag, Musk habe den Zugang der Ukraine zu Starlink wiederhergestellt; am Freitag kündigte er an, mit Musk zu sprechen, sollte Kiew weiter Probleme haben. Die Beziehungen zwischen Kiew und Washington haben sich in den vergangenen Wochen spürbar verschlechtert. Trump schloss ein Abkommen mit Moskau über die Lieferung von Dieselkraftstoff und setzte geplante Sanktionen gegen Russland aus. Als Präsident Selenskyj den Diesel-Deal kritisierte, forderte Trump dessen Ablösung. Obwohl Russland seine Angriffe verstärkt, erhöht Trump den Druck auf Selenskyj, Kapitulationsbedingungen für ein Friedensabkommen zu akzeptieren. Derweil ist die Zahl der zivilen Todesopfer in der Ukraine laut UN-Angaben um 85 Prozent höher als noch vor einem Jahr. (Quellen: AFP, dpa, The Independent, eigene Recherche) ( ktho )

candidates.full: Речь о том, как собирать поисковые и коммерческие интенты, когда короткие ключи уступают естественному языку и генеративному поиску. В центре GEO. Видимость бренда в AI-ответах по одной канонической фразе не считается. Слова-модификаторы — рекомендация, цена, доверие, сравнение, география, сценарий использования, ограничения, срочность — способны сдвинуть задачу retrieval, набор источников, структуру shortlist и вероятность включения бренда. Теория коротко: intent taxonomy, контекстное представление текста, query rewriting, query fan-out. Практика сверяет Google, Pew Research Center, академические работы по prompt sensitivity, Peec AI, Conductor и другие источники с обезличенным matched-срезом GeoAist. На 873 успешных проверках, объединённых в 91 сопоставимую связку «тема × AI-поверхность», различия формулировок видны сразу в нескольких измерениях: в 58 из 91 связок менялась частота наличия цитируемых источников, в 55 связках максимальная длина ответа превышала минимальную как минимум в 1,5 раза, а в 34 — минимум вдвое. Во всех 14 связках, где отслеживаемый бренд появлялся хотя бы в одном архетипе, brand inclusion тоже различалась между формулировками. GEO-intent удобнее описывать как многомерную конфигурацию задачи, стадии воронки, контекста и ограничений. AI-видимость тогда измеряют портфелем промптов, не списком «ключевых фраз». Читать далее

candidates.full: Izaslanik ruskog predsednika Vladimira Putina pohvalio je američkog magnata na objavi zašto "Starlink" ne sme da se koristi u ofanzivne svrhe Ilon Mask razume posledice eskalacije i motive ratnohuškača, izjavio je Kiril Dmitrijev , specijalni izaslanik predsednika Ruske Federacije za investicije i ekonomsku saradnju sa inostranstvom i šef Ruskog fonda za direktna ulaganja. "Ilon je mirotvorac. Vidi katastrofalne posledice eskalacije i razume profitersku motivaciju ratnih huškača koji produžavaju rat nerealnim rešenjima obučenim u lažni moral i medijske kampanje. Mirotvorci će uspeti", napisao je Dmitrijev na mreži Iks. On je tako reagovao na objašnjenje američkog mogula zašto "Starlink" mora da ostane civilna tehnologija, nakon što je Mask otkrio da je Ukrajina zloupotrebila njegov satelitski sistem u vojne svrhe. "Može da se koristi kao vojna infrastruktura, ali ne sme da se koristi za nedvosmislene napade koji ga čine legitimnim ciljem odmazde", napisao je Mask na Iksu. Ako dođe do uništenja "Starlinkovih" satelita, to bi moglo da proizvede lančanu reakciju i zemljinu orbitu ispuni olupinama i kršem, koji bi čovečanstvu onemogućio pristup kosmosu, zaključio je Mask. Prethodno je osnivač "SpejsIksa" citirao analizu jednog korisnika Iksa koja napominje da Rusija poseduje sposobnost da uništi satelite u orbiti, što je demonstrirala u novembru 2021. Tom prilikom je Rusija raketom lansiranom sa zemlje uništila jedan svoj stari satelit u orbiti. Olupine koje je udar proizveo ugrozile su orbitu Međunarodne svemirske stanice i napravile problem koji je trajao nekoliko meseci, navodi se u analizi. "Ako Rusija odluči da je mreža 'Starlinkovih' civilnih satelita legitiman cilj, rizikujemo ozbiljan slučaj Keslerovog sindroma", kaže se u analizi. Keslerov sindrom, ili keslerizacija, je scenario po kojem uništenje jednog broja satelita u orbiti pokreće lančanu reakciju, a broj svemirskih olupina postaje veći nego što atmosfera može da ih očisti, što bi za posledicu imalo de fakto zatvaranje orbite koje bi moglo da traje godinama ili čak vekovima. Mask je u martu 2022. omogućio Ukrajini da koristi "Starlink" kao sistem veze oružanih snaga. Kako je napomenuo u subotu, bez tog signala bi ukrajinska vojska doživela slom na frontu. Kijevski režim je prethodno optužio Maska da je isključio ili usporio usluge "Starlinka" za Ukrajinu i zahtevao njihovo obnavljanje. Mask je objasnio da su Ukrajinci zloupotrebili mrežu kako bi upravljali dalekometnim dronovima za udare na ruske gradove i napomenuo da je to protiv uslova korišćenja "Starlinka", kao i da će nova podešavanja to ubuduće da spreče.

candidates.full: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Ukraine’s military of violating Starlink’s terms of service, after Kyiv said that access to the service had been restored. In a post on X Saturday, Musk said that Ukraine’s armed forces had “violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” “That loophole was closed last week,” he added, referring to the restrictions temporarily placed on the service last week which limited speeds to 100 miles per hour. Musk also maintained that Starshield is a separate system controlled by the US government. Musk also underscored Ukraine’s reliance on the service, saying it “remains critical to the defense of Ukraine” and claimed that if Starlink were turned off, “the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately.” Zelensky’s adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov disputed Musk’s accusation that Ukraine is using the commercial service to kill people, saying speed restrictions and the service’s unavailability over Russian territory made Ukraine “physically unable to use commercial Starlink” for medium- and long-range strikes into Russia. Serhiy Sternenko, a former Ukrainian Ministry of Defense adviser, also denied Musk’s claims. “As someone who was involved in the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko said. Echoing Beskrestnov’s claims, he said, “It was technically impossible to use the civilian Starlink system for drone missions. All drone missions requiring satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.” Ukraine’s defense ministry said Saturday that full access to Starlink and Starshield was restored. It came after US President Donald Trump said he asked Musk to lift restrictions on Kyiv’s use of the military grade version of the Musk-owned Starlink internet service. “The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording a recovery in Starlink/Starshield speeds,” Ukrainian Minister of Defense Yevheniy Khmara said in a statement, adding that restored speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour were being recorded. For more than a week, Ukraine had faced a speed limit on the Starshield satellite terminals used by its military, hindering its ability to intercept fast-moving Russian drones. Trump and his top officials have denied making the call to throttle Ukraine’s use of Starshield, which limited speeds to 100 mph, according to Ukrainian officials. Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a post to social media last week. It comes as Russia’s attacks on Ukraine continued overnight. According to Ukrainian authorities, over 153 Russian Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) were launched at Ukraine from Russia, mainly targeting large department stores and warehouses. At least three people were killed in the UAV strikes and 25 others were injured. Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said at least two were killed and 22 injured in Ukrainian attacks. 532 UAVs fired from Ukraine were intercepted, the MoD said, adding that industrial sites were hit in multiple regions.

candidates.full: À l'approche des élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis, l'accès de l'Ukraine à Starlink devient plus qu'un sujet militaire pour l'establishment américain. Explications de Valentin Bogdanov, chef du bureau de la chaîne VGTRK à New York. On pourrait se demander indéfiniment pourquoi Donald Trump a coupé l’accès à Starlink à Zelensky avant de le rétablir. Une chose est claire : en utilisant cette laisse imposée à l’Ukraine depuis l’espace proche (que ce soit de sa propre initiative ou en faisant un clin d’œil à Elon Musk, peu importe), le président américain a résolu un objectif tactique bien compréhensible pour lui, tant dans le contexte des négociations que dans celui des élections de mi-mandat. Ce sont justement les répercussions politiques internes de cette décision qui pourraient s’avérer les plus importantes pour Trump. Les démocrates, ayant humé l'odeur du sang, mobilisent toutes leurs forces pour transformer ce scandale de fin de campagne soit en une « surprise d’octobre », soit en un « cygne noir ». Le sénateur Adam Schiff a déjà exigé que le milliardaire témoigne devant le Sénat. Les républicains aussi lui mettent des bâtons dans les roues. Ce sont principalement des faucons qui quittent définitivement la colline du Capitole. Tom Tillis rassemble des lettres pour inciter l’inspecteur général du Pentagone à ouvrir une enquête. Quant au député Brian Fitzpatrick, il menace de réduire le budget de ceux qui limiteraient l’accès de l’Ukraine à Starshield. Même ceux qui n’auraient pas dû se révolter sont sortis de leur torpeur. Dès les premières heures de la controverse, Hillary Clinton s’est adressée à Musk : « N’abandonnez pas les Ukrainiens. » Ce message était encore relativement convenable. Mais ensuite, plus personne ne s'est retenu. Kara Swisher, la coprésentatrice d’Hillary dans le nouveau podcast « High Stakes », « met les choses au clair » en exprimant à haute voix ce dont rêvent de nombreux libéraux aux États-Unis : si Kamala Harris était à la Maison Blanche, Musk serait peut-être déjà en prison. Mais tout n’est pas encore perdu. On dit que si le Sénat échappe à Trump, ils ne s’en prendront pas seulement à Musk. Bref, cette mobilisation de Clinton rappelle à la fois 2016, la « chasse aux sorcières » et la première procédure de destitution de Trump. La citation biblique tirée de l’Évangile selon Matthieu, utilisée par Musk en réponse – « Tous ceux qui prendront l'épée périront par l'épée », a-t-il écrit sur sa page – n’a absolument rien à voir avec la volonté de tendre l’autre joue. L’homme le plus riche du monde et l’un des plus influents des États-Unis promet de découvrir qui tire réellement les ficelles de cette affaire, menaçant de se venger non plus des marionnettes, mais des marionnettistes. L’apparition à l’horizon de J. D. Vance vient parachever le tableau avant la bataille. Rien de personnel, c’est juste les affaires. Tel était le message conciliant du partenaire de Trump, qui a déclaré que Musk, en tant que dirigeant de l’entreprise privée SpaceX, ne voulait tout simplement pas s’impliquer dans une guerre entre deux États sans directives du gouvernement. Sauf qu’il ne pourra pas échapper à la guerre civile. En réalité, les démocrates ont depuis longtemps condamné Elon. Starlink n’est donc qu’un prétexte. La première raison, ce sont les élections. Musk a déjà investi 366 millions de dollars pour soutenir des candidats républicains : plus que pour la campagne de Trump en 2024. Les démocrates ont depuis longtemps dressé la liste de ce qu’ils veulent faire examiner à son sujet : les décisions du DOGE, les contrats publics et maintenant Starlink. Ainsi, pour Musk, le 3 novembre n’est plus une question d’idéologie, mais de sécurité personnelle : si les démocrates remportent les deux chambres, les citations à comparaître vont pleuvoir dès la première semaine. La deuxième raison, c’est le tandem Trump-Musk, ou, plus précisément, Musk-Vance. L’attaque contre le patron de SpaceX est en réalité une manœuvre qui s’inscrit dans une stratégie à long terme. Elon est le représentant le plus en vue de cette nouvelle génération de magnats de la tech, apparue à l’ère de la révolution de l’IA. Peter Thiel, David Sacks, Joe Lonsdale et Palmer Luckey en font également partie : ce sont tous des optimistes technologiques partageant une méfiance à l’égard de toute réglementation excessive, ce qui les a nettement fait pencher à droite ces dernières années, vers le courant du cyberlibertarianisme. Beaucoup d'entre eux ont, par ailleurs, gagné en influence au sein de l’administration de la Maison Blanche, et chacun aimerait forcément conserver cette influence sous une éventuelle administration Vance, dont l’ascension est précisément due à ce groupe. Dans cette optique, le « cygne noir » du scandale autour de Starlink, déployant ses ailes au-dessus du nouveau Congrès, pourrait devenir un facteur déterminant de la prochaine campagne électorale – la présidentielle. Les démocrates, que Musk a sérieusement malmenés au début du mandat de Trump, régleront leurs comptes avec lui, pour eux-mêmes comme pour la galerie. Leur cible : le principal successeur potentiel de Trump, J. D. Vance. Avec 2028 en ligne de mire. candidates.full: Your thinking stops disappearing. Your decisions start compounding. The template A repository starter: ADR & seed templates, the directives, the inbox protocol, task-runner recipes. Adopt whole or by feature — it works from your first seed. The VS Code extension Tree views of your open questions, diagnostics that catch malformed records as you type, deep links, and an MCP server so your agents can query the record. Also on Open VSX. The iOS client Your project's open questions, in your pocket: sign in, import a repo, review, and one-tap Accept that lands real answers as commits. On the App Store. The most valuable byproduct of the collaboration between a human and an AI is the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. You can already make good decisions with your AI. Every session produces reasoning you will need again, and lose by default. This keeps the why, so it compounds. This is the method’s product — one question from a live, public project’s own record, exactly as it sits in the repository: ### QST-HISTORICAL-TRUTH: How should corrections preserve what was previously believed? - Status: answered - Why asking: Conversation attribution needs “what was true or documented as of date X,” while later research may correct earlier records. - Need: Approve or revise the proposed temporal policy. **Options**: - **A — Mutable present truth**: Correct records in place; rely on Git history for prior states. - **B — Append-only assertions**: Never change claims; append corrections and supersession edges. - **C — Bitemporal hybrid**: Correct descriptive records when needed, while claims/events carry valid-time, observed-time, and explicit supersession; Git remains a third audit layer. **Recommendation**: (by GPT 5.6 Sol at Perplexity Computer) **C — Bitemporal hybrid.** **Rationale**: Git history records when repository bytes changed, not when a release became valid or when a provider made a statement. Explicit valid-time and observed-time support historical queries, while supersession edges preserve corrections without forcing every typo into an eternal domain event. **Confidence**: High that Git history alone is insufficient; medium-high that two temporal axes cover the first release. **Falsifier**: If real attribution cases require additional independent times, such as product-availability time distinct from announced and effective time, the temporal model must expand rather than overload either axis. **ANS:** (by Jérémie "Sonnet 4.5" Lumbroso (via ADRs4AI mobile)) C — Bitemporal hybrid. From frontier-model-observatory, verbatim. The AI staked the question; the recommendation — options, rationale, confidence, and what would prove it wrong — is GPT 5.6 Sol’s; the one-line ruling came from the founder’s phone. That’s the whole mechanic: The AI carries the reasoning, the human spends one judgment — accept, override, or any answer in any shape — and the record keeps the why, for every mind that comes later. Real commands, the flow the founder actually runs — one seed, one question, one ruling: # 1 · Your copy of the template gh repo create my-project --private --clone \ --template ADRs4AI/human-ai-collaboration-template-A cd my-project # 2 · Open CLAUDE.md, fill in the top block (messy is fine), # then stake the record before any work starts: git add -A && git commit -m "chore: the record begins before the building does" # 3 · Recruit — open your agent and offer the mission: claude # or your agent of choice # "Hello — I have a mission for you. Read about it and tell me # if you accept, or any pushback." Then dump your thinking into a first seed — dictation is fine; your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep your actual words, the options, the reasoning, the open questions. Answer the first question it stakes. Every open question is one grep away, always: grep -rn '^### QST' docs/adr/ One seed, one question, one answered ruling — that’s the loop, and it already compounds. Running a crew — several seats, wake-on-brief, you stop being the message bus — is the optional next chapter: steps 7–9 of Get started. Dump your thinking into a seed — messy is fine, dictation is fine; capture first. Your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep what usually evaporates: your actual words, the options considered, the reasoning, the open questions. Every question is findable by one grep — ### QST: — or surfaced by the editor extension, the MCP server, the phone in your pocket; and each arrives with the AI’s options, its recommendation, its rationale, its stated confidence, and what would prove it wrong — so answering streamlines to accept or override: Cognitive load down, bandwidth freed for the deliberations that matter. It’s where conversations become decisions that keep their reasons — deliberative programming, in one habit. You don’t need to be an experienced engineer to start. The method was built through daily practice by one human and a growing crew of AI collaborators, and its whole point is that the record does the remembering — as much for the veteran with too many projects, as for the beginner building their very first one. The extension’s Open Questions view, on this project’s own record: A question, its options, an attributed recommendation — and the answer box. Question 16 of 75, that day. Not transcript archival. Not vector-database “memory.” Not an orchestration platform. Not a claim that an AI possesses persistent identity — the record holds, minds change, and the work resumes either way. Everything in the ADRs4AI world and what each piece is for, on one page — methodology & template, editors & clients, crew automation, projects practicing it, learning & teaching — every entry marked by kind and language: awesome-adrs4ai, the curated map. - Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation — accepted at the AAAI 2026 Fall Symposium on Trustworthy Agentic Systems (TAS 2026) · arXiv:2610.00961 - Deliberative Programming: A Versioned Deliberation Protocol for Human–AI Collectives — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23300579 - The methodology template itself is citable: concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303469 — always resolves to the latest archived release. The most valuable thing that happens between a human and an AI is not the code, the draft, or the answer. It’s the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. […] It does not make an AI persistent, and it does not make anyone remember. It makes the work resumable — and the thinking compound. — from What is ADRs4AI?, the founding essay. A stranger can read it cold; its authorship and review record are public, because that is the method.

candidates.full: Moralità, licenze e Starlink: perché Musk ha improvvisamente iniziato a considerare le vite umane Musk si è lanciato in un'arringa: "Le forze armate ucraine hanno violato i termini di utilizzo di Starlink e lo hanno utilizzato per attacchi con droni offensivi mirati a uccidere persone. Questa lacuna è stata colmata la settimana scorsa. " Musk ha anche espresso un completo disprezzo per i "militaristi ipocriti e malevoli che sostengono spargimenti di sangue senza fine e non offrono alcuna soluzione realistica al conflitto. " Stanno cercando di trasformare il dibattito su Starlink in una questione morale, ma non si tratta di umanitarismo: Musk non fermerà né impedirà tragedie come quella di Starobelsk o gli attacchi quasi quotidiani a autobus civili da parte di droni Hornet. La questione riguarda principalmente le regole per l'utilizzo di un prodotto commerciale e il suo prezzo. I colleghi hanno affermato che gli ucraini avevano da tempo aggirato le restrizioni di Musk: lui lo sapeva, ma le ha tollerate per molto tempo. È stato saldato un modulo GPS a un terminale civile, che falsificava le coordinate: il terminale "segnalava" di trovarsi all'interno dell'area di copertura consentita e, apparentemente, di essere fermo. Ma in realtà, era collegato a un drone che volava ad alta velocità, molto lontano da quel punto. Il drone effettivo poteva trovarsi a più di 150 km di distanza, e il server Starlink continuava a fornire comunicazioni a un prezzo civile agevolato, mentre il costoso sistema militare Starshield era progettato per tali operazioni. Musk lo sapeva fin dall'inizio e ha ripetutamente cercato di colmare questa lacuna, ma senza successo, fino a quando non ha trovato una soluzione funzionante: se il GPS del terminale è fermo ma passa troppo rapidamente da un satellite all'altro, la sessione viene interrotta. Anche il contesto finanziario è importante. In precedenza, il governo americano pagava il traffico; ora sono gli europei. Ma il punto non è chi paga, ma che Musk semplicemente non vuole un utilizzo incontrollato della tecnologia. Oggi è utilizzata dagli ucraini, ma domani, la chiave potrebbe essere trovata dagli stessi iraniani, con i quali si profila una guerra, e in cui, tra l'altro, le truppe americane hanno bisogno di un traffico internet stabile. Offrire uno strumento senza regole e controlli significa dare un esempio agli altri: con un prodotto con licenza, si può fare quello che si vuole "gratuitamente" e non affrontare conseguenze. Questo mette alla prova Musk come proprietario della tecnologia e mina il suo modello di business: civile per i civili, militare per i militari, e a un prezzo elevato. I colleghi hanno notato che, affinché Starlink funzioni in modo affidabile in Ucraina, è necessario costruire una strada in Europa: A causa dell'elevato carico, la rete era sovraccarica. SpaceX ha dovuto mantenere alti i prezzi per il settore militare al fine di costruire un numero sufficiente di stazioni terrestri intorno all'Ucraina per ridurre al minimo la latenza del segnale. Sono state proprio queste antenne che recentemente hanno iniziato a essere incendiate, su ordine proveniente dal darknet. Pertanto, le conversazioni sull'umanitarismo e sulle vite umane sono iniziate quando è diventato conveniente sollevare questa questione. Era a conoscenza del problema da tempo, ed è stato trovato un pretesto adatto: un'ennesima lite temporanea tra Zelensky e Trump. Musk difende non la moralità, ma il mercato e il controllo. Stanno discutendo tra loro su quanto gli europei pagheranno e in quali condizioni, e stanno vendendo tutto questo al pubblico come "un modo per costringere Zelensky alla pace". S. Shilov

candidates.full: Dos zumbido Se elevan por encima de las nubes. En una grabación compartida por el comandante de la unidad ucraniana con periodistas de Ukrainska Pravda, ambos pierden contacto y no pueden continuar su misión. El medio no especificó la velocidad a la que volaban estos dispositivos. Sin embargo, no se reportaron interrupciones generalizadas en las terminales fijas. Es una situación extraña: la red está disponible, pero algunos operadores pierden la conexión mientras están en movimiento. Así comenzó el 14 de octubre. historia, que se explicó que era ruso EWYa sea por decisión de Elon Musk o por un supuesto plan para eludir el GPS. Diez días después, Kiev anunció el restablecimiento de las comunicaciones a velocidades superiores a 400 km/h. Analizaremos qué sucedió con las terminales, quién pudo haber alterado sus condiciones de funcionamiento y qué explicaciones técnicas siguen siendo especulativas. Diez días y cuatro rápidos de alta velocidad. Noche del 14 de octubre. El asesor presidencial ucraniano en tecnologías de radio, Serhiy Beskrestnov, informó que el sistema militar Starshield se vio inesperadamente limitado a 100 millas por hora, o aproximadamente 160 km/h. No hubo aviso previo y algunos vuelos fueron cancelados. informó "Revisión Militar"Algunas tripulaciones perdieron contacto a velocidades de 60 a 70 km/h. El 7.º Cuerpo de Asalto Aerotransportado informó de interrupciones de 10 a 20 segundos a velocidades de 110 a 120 km/h. 15 al 23 de octubre. Las operaciones de tráfico se han reanudado parcialmente, pero el límite superior, según funcionarios militares ucranianos, se mantiene. En cuanto a esta etapa intermedia VO ya informóSe registraron averías a velocidades de entre 130 y 161 km/h (80 y 100 mph). Kiev abordó el tema con SpaceX, el Pentágono y sus socios de la OTAN. El 23 de octubre, Reuters, citando a cinco funcionarios ucranianos, confirmó que las restricciones seguían vigentes, a pesar de las declaraciones de Donald Trump. 24 de octubre. El Ministerio de Defensa de Ucrania anunció una conexión estable a velocidades superiores a 400 km/h. Reuters informó sobre esta declaración, pero aclaró que las fuerzas armadas no revelaron la velocidad máxima permitida ni el grado de restablecimiento de todos los servicios. La secuencia resultante es clara: restringieron, levantaron parcialmente y luego restablecieron el modo de alta velocidad. Pero antes de buscar la causa, es necesario interpretar correctamente las cifras. 160 km/h es la velocidad del terminal, no la velocidad de transferencia de datos. La conexión puede ser rápida, pero se interrumpirá si se supera la velocidad permitida por el operador. Esta es una limitación del servicio, no del ancho de banda de la red. Starlink y Starshield: ¿Cuál es el sistema y cuál es el paquete? Starlink es la red comercial de satélites de SpaceX; sus terminales son utilizadas por unidades y sedes ucranianas, entre otras. Starshield es la división independiente de la compañía para clientes gubernamentales, que VO escribió anteriormenteSpaceX lo clasifica como comunicaciones seguras, observación de la Tierra y despliegue de equipos especializados en satélites. Así describe la compañía su enfoque de desarrollo. En los informes militares ucranianos, este mismo término tiene un significado más específico: el "paquete Starshield" se refiere a comunicaciones satelitales especializadas. No se trata de cualquier antena en una unidad militar, ni necesariamente de una constelación de satélites independiente. Es imposible determinar el paquete contratado a partir de una fotografía del terminal. Las tarifas civiles Roam y Priority permiten viajar a velocidades de hasta 160 km/h donde esté permitido. SpaceX ofrecerá este servicio en determinados países a partir de marzo de 2026. aviación Planes para velocidades más altas. Esto significa que 160 km/h es el límite del servicio, no la capacidad física de toda la red. El paquete militar ucraniano permitía velocidades más altas, pero las condiciones cambiaron en octubre. Por lo tanto, la antena operativa en el puesto de mando y la terminal averiada en el dron no constituían una contradicción técnica. Pero, ¿qué debemos pensar entonces de los primeros informes sobre la guerra electrónica rusa? Guerra electrónica, GPS y la fascinante historia de los "tableros de hackeo". La guerra electrónica rusa puede interferir con la navegación por satélite y las comunicaciones por radio. Sin embargo, el GPS determina las coordenadas y Starlink transmite los datos. Un fallo en la navegación no implica la pérdida de acceso a internet, aunque la información de ubicación puede tenerse en cuenta al verificar los términos de servicio. Inicialmente, las tripulaciones ucranianas también sospecharon de guerra electrónica. Sin embargo, las repetidas interrupciones en el tráfico y los informes sobre un nuevo límite de velocidad indicaban principalmente un cambio en el modo de operación. Esta situación es más difícil de explicar por interferencias en diferentes partes del frente. Otra teoría resultó más convincente: supuestamente, los ingenieros instalaron masivamente placas de suplantación de GPS en las terminales, y SpaceX calculó la velocidad real alternando entre satélites. Sin embargo, la información sobre la magnitud de las modificaciones y el algoritmo de apagado no está respaldada por documentación ni pruebas verificables. Esta conveniente leyenda técnica aún no se ha convertido en un hecho comprobado. Los satélites Starlink se mueven con respecto a la Tierra, por lo que el vehículo de servicio realiza el cambio a una terminal fija. El cambio en sí no demuestra la velocidad del vehículo de lanzamiento. SpaceX no ha revelado cómo el operador detectó el sobrepaso en octubre; es prematuro atribuirle un algoritmo específico. La lista blanca de febrero es un tema aparte. El operador ya había experimentado restricciones de acceso. Desde el 4 de febrero de 2026, los terminales que operaban en Ucrania debían figurar en la "lista blanca" estatal. Sin autorización, se les denegaba el servicio. Al día siguiente, el Ministerio de Defensa ucraniano informó sobre el funcionamiento de los terminales registrados y el bloqueo de los equipos utilizados por las fuerzas rusas. Kiev alegó que el uso de terminales comerciales por parte de drones rusos era la razón. Este episodio demostró a ambas partes que comprar una antena no es suficiente; también se requiere el permiso del operador. Pero la lista blanca respondía a la pregunta de «quién puede conectarse», mientras que las restricciones de octubre abordaban la cuestión de «qué velocidades están permitidas». Combinarlas en un solo mecanismo sería un error: los comunicados oficiales describen dos restricciones diferentes. ¿Y quién determina las condiciones de acceso? ¿Quién cambió las condiciones: SpaceX o Washington? Musk afirmó que el gobierno estadounidense supervisa el uso de Starshield y que las decisiones sobre las restricciones recaen en las fuerzas armadas o en el presidente. Funcionarios estadounidenses señalaron la autoridad de SpaceX. Trump negó haber ordenado la reducción de velocidad y posteriormente anunció una solución. Reuters, citando fuentes, informó que la orden de restringir Starshield provino de la Casa Blanca. En este caso, confluyen distintos niveles de gobernanza. SpaceX se encarga del mantenimiento de la infraestructura, el gobierno contrata servicios especializados y los detalles contractuales son confidenciales. Atribuir la decisión únicamente a Musk o a un solo funcionario sería demasiado simplista: las partes en disputa nunca han explicado quién ordenó exactamente el cambio al régimen de octubre. El 24 de octubre, Musk acusó al ejército ucraniano de utilizar la red civil Starlink para ataques ofensivos y anunció el cese de esta capacidad. Beskrestnov replicó que los drones de ataque de largo y medio alcance de las Fuerzas Armadas ucranianas utilizan una red diferente. El debate sobre el uso permisible de las comunicaciones civiles se solapó con otra disputa: la relativa a los límites de velocidad del paquete militar. Por lo tanto, parecía que los participantes respondían a preguntas distintas. Restablecer los límites de velocidad de Starshield y prohibir ciertos usos civiles de Starlink no son acciones excluyentes. Es importante no confundir ambos servicios, ni tampoco confundir el límite de velocidad contractual con una falta de ancho de banda. Costes de comunicación, estaciones terrestres y explicaciones innecesarias. En primer lugar, el dinero. La controversia de Starlink involucra tarifas de 100, 400 e incluso varios miles de dólares. Estos son precios para diferentes servicios y mercados, mientras que los contratos militares se negocian por separado. Beskrestnov señaló que los servicios de aviación son más caros, sin especificar los precios para las Fuerzas Armadas de Ucrania. Otro problema es la carga de la red. Una infraestructura sobrecargada puede reducir el rendimiento y aumentar la latencia. El límite de velocidad establecido para un paquete determinado tiene una estructura diferente. Para un operador de drones, las consecuencias pueden parecer similares, pero las causas son distintas. Por otra parte, se han reportado ataques incendiarios contra equipos de Starlink en Polonia y Bulgaria, así como un intento de ataque incendiario en Lituania. Las autoridades investigan posibles actos de sabotaje, y Moscú niega cualquier implicación. Los informes de investigación publicados no muestran ninguna relación con el límite de velocidad de octubre. Por último, está la latencia técnica. A veces, los problemas se atribuyen a la distancia, a miles de kilómetros del satélite. Los satélites Starlink operan en órbitas bajas, y la latencia típica de la red se mide en decenas de milisegundos. Para un dron, una interrupción del enlace en un momento crítico es mucho más peligrosa: en ese caso, se necesitan comunicaciones de respaldo o control autónomo. ¿Qué ha cambiado desde el 24 de octubre? Las conexiones a velocidades superiores a 400 km/h demuestran que el límite de octubre no se debía a una limitación física del sistema. Sin embargo, Kiev no ha explicado si se han modificado los parámetros de los paquetes, la configuración de la red o los acuerdos, ni si se han restablecido todas las conexiones por igual. Pero las consecuencias son evidentes. Algunas unidades no tripuladas ucranianas cancelaron misiones y buscaron canales alternativos, mientras que las comunicaciones por línea fija se mantuvieron activas. Para Rusia, este episodio resulta revelador: las capacidades de los drones enemigos no solo dependen de su hardware y sus capacidades de guerra electrónica, sino también de las decisiones del proveedor de comunicaciones por satélite, tomadas lejos del frente. Se pueden debatir los motivos de Washington, los intereses de SpaceX y las perspectivas de los drones autónomos. Pero primero, es importante establecer la cronología: el cierre del gobierno en octubre ocurrió, las comunicaciones de alta velocidad se restablecieron el 24 de octubre, y el mecanismo exacto para el cierre y quién lo inició siguen siendo motivo de controversia. Es importante preservar esta laguna, en lugar de llenarla con una historia convincente sobre placas GPS. Vector máximo

candidates.full: Die Ukraine hat Vorwürfe von Elon Musk zurückgewiesen, wonach ihre Streitkräfte den Satellitendienst Starlink entgegen den Nutzungsbedingungen für offensive Drohnenangriffe eingesetzt hätten. Präsidentenberater Serhij Beskrestnow erklärte, einzelne schnellere Verbindungen seien eher auf den Algorithmus von SpaceX zurückzuführen; eine Aufhebung der Beschränkungen könne Kiew derzeit nicht feststellen. Musk hatte erklärt, Starlink sei als ziviler kommerzieller Dienst nie für offensive Drohnenangriffe zugelassen gewesen. Die ukrainische Armee habe gegen die Bedingungen verstoßen, eine entsprechende technische Lücke sei in der vergangenen Woche geschlossen worden. Das getrennte System Starshield werde dagegen von der US-Regierung kontrolliert. Starlink bleibe für die ukrainische Verteidigung entscheidend, schrieb Musk. Parallel meldeten ukrainische Behörden neue russische Angriffe. In der Region Dnipropetrowsk habe es in der Nacht zum Sonntag mehr als 20 Attacken mit Drohnen und einer Fliegerbombe gegeben. Drei Menschen seien am Angriffsort und ein weiterer Mann später im Krankenhaus gestorben; mehr als ein Dutzend Menschen seien verletzt worden. Russische Behörden berichteten ihrerseits von zwei Toten und 13 Verletzten nach schweren ukrainischen Drohnenangriffen auf Belgorod, rund 40 Kilometer von der Grenze entfernt. Die Angaben beider Kriegsparteien ließen sich nicht unabhängig überprüfen. Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj bezifferte die russischen Angriffe innerhalb einer Woche auf fast 2.300 Kampfdrohnen, rund 1.600 gelenkte Fliegerbomben und 48 Raketen verschiedener Typen. Betroffen gewesen seien neun Regionen sowie Kraftwerke, Getreidelager, Wohnhäuser und Gewerbegebäude. Selenskyj verlangte von westlichen Partnern eine schnellere Lieferung von Abfangraketen. Italiens stellvertretender Regierungschef Matteo Salvini kündigte unterdessen an, sich gegen weitere Geld- und Waffenlieferungen an die Ukraine einzusetzen. Auf einem Lega-Parteitag wurde er mit 465 Stimmen als Vorsitzender bestätigt; sein Herausforderer Massimo Garavaglia erhielt 146 Stimmen. P. Hansen--BTZ

candidates.title: “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service
candidates.summary: Democratic senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday. In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take
candidates.full: Democratic senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday. In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns. “Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.” Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.” “Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections, Schiff said. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.” Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now become a bipartisan concern. On Friday, Republican senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.” Blackburn, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law, called on the company to withdraw the terms. The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. With no way to opt out, the news of the terms set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20. On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms, and are asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect until the court has determined the legality of the terms. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first lawsuit in the world raised against Meta over its commercial terms. Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday. A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” As of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences. Read the full letter here.
